chunks.text: Alstonia scholaris — called blackboard tree, scholar tree, devil tree or (in India) saptaparni/saptaparna, 'seven leaves', for its whorls of typically seven leaves — is a large evergreen Apocynaceae tree reaching up to 40 m, rarely 60 m, with a buttressed, fluted trunk and milky latex in every part. It bears cream or white, strongly and sweetly scented tubular flowers in branched terminal clusters, followed by long paired papery seed pods. Native from Pakistan across South and Southeast Asia to northern Australia, it is IUCN-rated Least Concern. Traditional use of its bitter bark against bowel complaints, chronic diarrhoea, dysentery and malaria-like fevers is documented as far back as an 1889 text, though modern testing found its antimalarial activity against Plasmodium falciparum very weak; the bark alkaloid echitamine is nonetheless still sold commercially as a herbal medicine. The tree is West Bengal's state tree, and Visva-Bharati University — the institution founded by Rabindranath Tagore — continues his tradition of presenting graduating students with a saptaparni leaf at convocation. The wood is recommended for pencil manufacture because the tree grows fast and is easy to cultivate, and the plant as a whole is toxic in concentrated extract, with documented organ damage in animal studies and marked seasonal variation in toxicity (summer bark being the most toxic).

chunks.source: Down To Earth — 'Not all green is healthy' (1992)
chunks.text: This 1992 investigative report is useful precisely because it shows the pollen-allergy concern around Alstonia scholaris to be older, murkier and less settled than popular belief suggests. It describes a real controversy at IIT Kanpur, where about ten of the roughly 1,000 Alstonia trees on campus were felled after staff complained of asthma attacks, sparking protests from environmentally minded staff — but it also quotes allergy expert A.B. Singh of New Delhi's Centre for Biochemicals saying that, as of that writing, no study had actually demonstrated Alstonia pollen to be an allergen, and criticising India's afforestation programmes for planting exotic species without first screening their allergenic potential (he pointed instead to mulberry, Morus alba, as a species with documented but under-regulated allergenic pollen in India). The article situates this within a broader picture: roughly 10% of India's population had major allergic disorders at the time, about 4% allergic rhinitis and over 1% bronchial asthma, and allergen content in the same species can vary significantly by region and climate. In short, the Alstonia-as-allergen narrative common in Indian cities is longstanding and plausible but, per this source, was not conclusively proven even as of its publication — a nuance worth preserving rather than flattening into a settled 'fact'.
